words.lemma: ἕννυμι (corpus lemma ἵζω is a mislemmatization)

cognate: Ved. amṛ́ta- = Gk ἄμβροτος/ἀμβρόσιος (*n̥-mr̥-tó- 'immortal'); Ved. vas- 'clothe, wear' = Gk ἕννυμι, εἷμα, ἑανός (*wes-)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic uses the substantivized neuter amṛ́ta- ('the immortal, immortality') as the thing worn (acc. with middle vásāna-, instr. with ánu vas-); Greek makes it an adjective on a garment noun from the same root (ἄμβροτα εἵματα, ἀμβρόσιος ἑανός), a figura etymologica with the verb.
shared_syntax: verb *wes- 'clothe/put on' + *n̥mr̥tó- as what is worn: transitive causative 'clothe X with the immortal' (RV ánu vastām amŕ̥tena ~ Il. ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσε) and middle 'wearing the immortal' (AV amṛtam vasānā ~ Il. 14.178 ἀμβρόσιον ἑανὸν ἕσατο).
context: RV 6.75.18 = AVŚ 7.118.1 closes the weapons hymn: the warrior's vital points are covered with armour and King Soma is to clothe him with immortality, i.e. dress that keeps death off. In Il. 16.670/680 Apollo washes Sarpedon's corpse, anoints it with ambrosia and dresses it in immortal garments; in Od. 24.59 the Nereids dress Achilles' corpse the same way. Both traditions put the formula in a fallen or endangered warrior's body being dressed by a god against death and its decay. AVŚ 9.1.2 (the honey-whip 'wearing amṛta') and Il. 14.178 (Hera's ambrosial robe) show the middle 'wear the immortal' of divine beings. Caveat: both *n̥mr̥tó- epithets attach to many divine things (ἄμβροτος of hair, blood, night), so some chance pairing with clothing is possible. That is why this is medium and not high, although the collocation is formulaic on both sides (6 Homeric loci in two line shapes; three Vedic loci).

support.locus: RV 10.87.16 / AVŚ 8.3.29 (av:AVŚ, 8, 3.s29 in this slab, B-5f6e0)

cognate: Ved. āma- = Gk ὠμός (*h₂eh₃mó- 'raw'); Ved. kravís- = Gk κρέας (*kréwh₂s 'raw flesh'); Ved. ad- = Gk ἔδω (*h₁ed- 'eat'); agent compounds Ved. āmā́d- ~ Gk ὠμηστής (*h₂eh₃mo-h₁ed-) and kravyā́d-
drift_or_renewal: In the AV line āma- qualifies the inherited Indo-Iranian māṃsá- (*mḗms), and kravís- stands as a second object ('human kravis'); Greek has the adjective directly on κρέα. So the three roots form one clause in both, not one identical NP.
shared_syntax: verb *h₁ed- with object 'raw flesh' (*h₂eh₃mó- + flesh noun, *kréwh₂s in both): AV āmaṃ māṃsam adanti ... kraviḥ ~ Il. ὤμ' ... κρέα ἔδμεναι
context: Both describe eating raw human flesh as the mark of something monstrous: AV 8.6.48 names the demons 'who eat raw meat and who eat human kravis'; Il. 22.347 has Achilles, at his most savage, wishing he could cut up Hector's flesh and eat it raw. Both traditions also attach the curse that a foe's body will be eaten raw by beasts, with matching agent compounds: RV 10.87.7 'let the raw-eating (āmā́daḥ) kṣviṅkā birds eat him' ~ Il. 11.454 'raw-eating birds (οἰωνοὶ ὠμησταί) will tear you'; ὠμηστής is also the dogs of Il. 22.67 and Achilles himself in 24.207, as kravyā́d- is the corpse-fire and the demons. Caveat: 'eat raw meat' is also ordinary language: in this slab's own bundle, Hippocrates De prisca medicina 13 has κρέα ὠμὰ ... ἐσθιέτω as dietetics. The case rests on the shared cannibal/curse context and the compounds, so medium.

words.etymon: déh₃- (or dʰeh₁-; Avestan dā- merges both)

cognate: Gk δίδωμι, δωτήρ, δώτωρ = Av. dā-, dātar- = Ved. dā-, dātár- (*deh₃-); Gk ἐΰς gen.pl. ἑάων = Av. vohu- = Ved. vásu- (*h₁wésu- 'good, goods')
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes. The slab anchors show the finite-verb form (δίδωσι ... ἑάων; dā̊s ... yā vohū); the agent-noun formula proper (*doh₃tōr h₁wesuom) is in the support loci.
shared_syntax: *deh₃- 'give' with *h₁wésu- 'good things' as object/genitive, said of gods: Il. 24.528 'gifts ... which (Zeus) gives, of bad things, and the other jar of goods (ἑάων)'; Y39.4 'as you, Ahura Mazdā, have thought, spoken, given/established and done the good things (yā vohū)'. Agent noun + gen.pl.: RV dātā́ vásūnām ~ Y65.12 vohunąm dātārō ~ Od. 8.325 δωτῆρες ἑάων.
context: Both anchors are about what the supreme god dispenses to men: Zeus's two jars in Achilles' speech to Priam, and Ahura Mazdā's good acts in the Yasna Haptaŋhāiti. The formula's distinctive features hold across the support: the archaic gen.pl. ἑάων, found only in this formula and this passage, matches vásūnām and vohunąm; and the plural divine collective 'gods, givers of goods' (Od. 8.325 θεοὶ δωτῆρες ἑάων) matches Y65.12 'Aməṣ̌a Spəṇtas ... givers of goods' (vohunąm dātārō). The AV pivot (svā vasūni) only gives the noun. The formula is high-grade, but the slab anchors are the verbal variant, so medium.

cognate: Ved. áṃsa- = Umbr. onse (loc.) = Gk ὦμος (*h₂ómso-); Ved. bhar- = Umbr. fer- = Gk φέρω (*bʰer-); Ved. ā-dhā- = Gk τίθημι (*dʰeh₁-)
shared_syntax: locative of 'shoulder' + *bʰer- 'carry': AV aṃse ādhāya bibhrati 'having put on the shoulder they carry' ~ Umbr. destre onse fertu 'let him carry on the right shoulder'; Greek has both verbs (ὤμοισι φόρησεν; ἐπ' ὤμου φέρειν; ἀμφ' ὤμοισι θέτο)
context: Exact cognates in the same case and verb relation, but the contexts do not match: AV 8.6.26 describes demons carrying their own bodies on the shoulder; the Iguvine line is a ritual instruction for carrying an implement; the Greek loci are arming scenes and Odysseus carrying a stag. Carrying on the shoulder is a universal action that any language describes with its ordinary words for shoulder and carry, so independent formation is likely. Recorded only because the match is three-way and exact in morphology (locative + *bʰer-).

note: All 161 bundles read. Most are prose/shared-root noise (Aristotle, Hippocrates, Cato). Four claims: immortal-clothing (medium), raw-flesh eating (medium), giver of goods (medium, recalled; the slab anchors are verbal), shoulder-carry (low). Considered and rejected: sleep/wake merism, cattle+sheep, tvac~σάκος, golden hall (one branch only), father/mother pairs.
